title: Search a 2D Matrix — binary search on flattened or top-right elimination.
shortTitle: Search a 2D Matrix — binary search on a conceptually flattened grid

s1_definition.profdef: Searching a sorted 2D matrix means finding whether a target value exists in a matrix whose rows are sorted left to right and whose first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Because the whole matrix is in effect one sorted sequence wrapped into rows, you can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array by mapping a one-dimensional index back to a row and column with integer division and modulo, giving O(log of (m times n)) time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India prints a giant ledger where every page has transaction amounts sorted smallest to largest, and the last amount on page one is always smaller than the first amount on page two. Rajesh wants to know if an amount of exactly 50000 rupees appears anywhere. Instead of reading every page, he treats all pages as one long sorted list, jumps to the middle, and decides whether to look in the earlier half or the later half, cutting the search in half each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: A fully sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search with index-to-row-column mapping finds any value in logarithmic time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Searching a sorted 2D matrix means finding whether a target value exists in a matrix whose rows are sorted left to right and whose first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Because the whole matrix is in effect one sorted sequence wrapped into rows, you can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array by mapping a one-dimensional index back to a row and column with integer division and modulo, giving O(log of (m times n)) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India prints a giant ledger where every page has transaction amounts sorted smallest to largest, and the last amount on page one is always smaller than the first amount on page two. Rajesh wants to know if an amount of exactly 50000 rupees appears anywhere. Instead of reading every page, he treats all pages as one long sorted list, jumps to the middle, and decides whether to look in the earlier half or the later half, cutting the search in half each time.

**One line to remember:** A fully sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search with index-to-row-column mapping finds any value in logarithmic time.

sections.s2_technical:
The matrix has `m` rows and `n` columns. The key property is global sorting: reading row by row gives a non-decreasing sequence. That lets us pretend the matrix is a single array of length `m * n`.

A binary search keeps two pointers `low = 0` and `high = m * n - 1`. The middle index `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` is computed the safe way to avoid integer overflow. To read the value at a flattened index, we convert it: the row is `mid / n` and the column is `mid % n`. For example, in a 3-by-4 matrix, flattened index 6 maps to row `6 / 4 = 1` and column `6 % 4 = 2`.

We compare `matrix[row][col]` with the target. If equal, we found it. If the value is smaller than the target, we move `low = mid + 1`. If larger, we move `high = mid - 1`. The loop ends when `low` passes `high`, meaning the value is absent.

A senior nuance: the `low + (high - low) / 2` form matters in real systems where the matrix could be large; `(low + high) / 2` can overflow a 32-bit int. Another nuance is that this approach only works when the matrix is globally sorted. If only each row is sorted but rows do not chain together, you must use the top-right elimination method instead, which is O(m + n).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs an end-of-day settlement report as a grid. Each row holds a block of settled transaction amounts, sorted ascending, and the blocks are themselves ordered so block two always starts above where block one ended. The compliance officer, Priya, needs a fast "does this exact amount exist" check while auditing, because scanning the entire grid for every query is too slow when there are millions of entries.

This is exactly how binary search on a flattened sorted matrix works. Because the grid is globally sorted, we can treat it as one long sorted array and halve the search space every step instead of scanning linearly.

Problem 2 — The officer must never get a wrong answer due to an arithmetic bug. If the midpoint calculation overflowed on a very large grid, the search could crash or return a false negative, which in a bank audit is unacceptable.

This is exactly why we use the overflow-safe midpoint formula and the clean index-to-coordinate mapping, so the search is both correct and fast.

The code will have an `Account` class for context, a `SettlementMatrixSearch` class with a `contains` method that runs the binary search, and a runnable demo that builds a sorted grid of settled amounts and queries for both present and absent values with logging at each decision.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 globally sorted grid and the target value 50000.

Step 1: The search computes `low = 0` and `high = 11` because the grid has twelve cells. The data lives entirely in the matrix; the pointers are just integers describing the search window.

Step 2: The midpoint is `0 + (11 - 0) / 2 = 5`. Mapping index 5 gives row `5 / 4 = 1` and column `5 % 4 = 1`, which is `matrix[1][1] = 50000`. That equals the target, so the method returns true immediately.

Step 3: For the absent target 55555, the first probe at index 5 reads 50000, which is smaller, so `low` becomes 6. The next midpoint is `6 + (11 - 6) / 2 = 8`, mapping to row 2 column 0, value 71000, which is larger, so `high` becomes 7. The next midpoint is `6 + (7 - 6) / 2 = 6`, value 58000, larger, so `high` becomes 5. Now `low (6)` is greater than `high (5)`, the loop ends, and the method returns false.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:30:00 INFO    Audit started by Priya Sharma on grid of 12 settled amounts
2026-10-27 12:30:00 INFO    Amount 50000 present? true (reconciles with SAV2001 transfer)
2026-10-27 12:30:00 INFO    Amount 55555 present? false
```

```

    │  grid is 3x4, globally sorted, 12 cells
    ▼
  Binary Search Window
    │ low=0, high=11
    ▼
  Probe mid=5 ──→ map 5 -> [1][1] = 50000
    │
    ├─ value == target (50000) ───→ return TRUE
    │
    └─ (for target 55555)
         value 50000 < 55555 → low=6
         probe mid=8 -> [2][0]=71000 > target → high=7
         probe mid=6 -> [1][2]=58000 > target → high=5
         low(6) > high(5) → return FALSE
    ▼
  Result delivered to compliance audit
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Searching a sorted two-dimensional matrix is a problem where every row is sorted left to right and the first element of each row is larger than the last element of the previous row, which means the entire matrix behaves like one long sorted array that has simply been folded into rows. Because of that global ordering, I can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array of length rows times columns, and the whole lookup finishes in logarithmic time rather than scanning every cell.

The technique that makes this work cleanly is the mapping from a one-dimensional index back to a row and a column. I keep a low pointer and a high pointer, I compute the midpoint using the overflow-safe form of low plus high minus low divided by two, and then I convert that midpoint into a row by integer division by the number of columns and into a column by the remainder. I compare the value there with the target and move the low pointer up or the high pointer down accordingly.

I always use the overflow-safe midpoint because on a very large grid the naive addition of low and high can exceed the range of a thirty-two bit integer, which in a banking audit could silently produce a wrong answer. I also make sure the matrix is genuinely globally sorted before I use this method, because if only each row is sorted and the rows do not chain together, I would instead start from the top-right corner and eliminate one row or one column per step, which runs in order rows plus columns time.

In my project at National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement report was stored as exactly this kind of globally sorted grid of settled amounts, and the compliance officer needed an instant check for whether a specific amount had settled. The flattened binary search gave that answer in a handful of comparisons even on grids with millions of entries, which kept the audit interactive instead of forcing a full scan for every query.
